What I found was the opposite.

The historians’ accounts of all three men show not only that they were sincere Muslims, but that they were known for serious religious devotion and trusted for it.

I found no historian of Islamic sects—not al-Shahrastānī, al-Baghdādī or al-Isfarāyīnī—who attacked the personal religious commitment of any of the three.

As for Maʿbad al-Juhanī, al-Isfarāyīnī speaks of him in a way that shows he was a transmitter of sayings from the Prophet.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
That alone gave him a respected religious standing and makes it difficult to accuse him of hostility toward Islam.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
It was even said that Ibn Mājah, one of the well-known transmitters of hadith, narrated some reports from him.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

If Maʿbad had not possessed this kind of Islamic religious standing, he could hardly have exercised the wide influence we have already described in major centers of Islamic learning such as Basra, Medina and Syria.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Nor would one of the great historians of Islamic sects, al-Dhahabī, have described him in his Mīzān al-Dhahab as a truthful member of the generation of the Successors.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The Successors ranked immediately after the Companions as trusted sources for reports from the Prophet used in Islamic law.

Even a modern Ashʿarite researcher admits that Maʿbad “was deeply religious,” despite the fact that Ashʿarites were among the strongest opponents of the Qadarites and of their later Muʿtazilite successors.

As for ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ, the fact that he was chosen to teach one of the sons of the Umayyad caliphs—Muʿāwiya ibn Yazīd—about religion shows that he was known as a religious scholar and teacher whose faith and knowledge were not in doubt.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The later accusation by the Umayyads that he had “corrupted” his student Muʿāwiya ibn Yazīd came only after the political crisis.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Their anger came from the fact that ʿAmr had taught one of their own sons an ideology opposed to the ideology of Umayyad rule.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
As a result, one member of the Umayyad family publicly exposed the wrongs of their political system.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The issue here was therefore political.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The killing of ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ was a political killing.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
As for Ghaylān al-Dimashqī, it is enough to note the trust placed in him by ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The caliph asked Ghaylān to help him reform Muslim affairs and placed him in charge of selling the Umayyad treasures.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
He did this even though he knew Ghaylān was a Qadarite and disagreed with him over the problem of human freedom.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
And we know that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz followed a religious path very different from that of the earlier Umayyad caliphs.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Al-Baghdādī also reports that al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥanafiyya used to say of Ghaylān:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“He is God’s proof against the people of Syria, but the young man will be killed.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This is the testimony of an important Muslim figure to Ghaylān’s high religious standing.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
There is something especially striking about Ghaylān.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
He grew up in Damascus, in an environment shaped by the pro-ʿUthmān party and by the Umayyads themselves.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

In other words, he grew up in an environment dominated by the ideology of divine compulsion, which worked hard to spread the claim that everything done by the Umayyads, good or bad, happened by God’s decree.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Yet Ghaylān was not absorbed into this environment or its ideology.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Instead, he openly opposed it with great passion and was eventually killed because of that opposition.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥanafiyya had predicted this fate.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Perhaps that prediction came from what was already known in Iraq and the Hijaz about Ghaylān’s passionate opposition to Umayyad determinism.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
He openly taught the opposite view: good deeds and goodness come from God, while evil deeds and wrongdoing come from human beings themselves.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
There is another historical point that supports our conclusion that these three Qadarites were not opposing Islam through their doctrine.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Rather, they were opposing the Umayyad rulers’ use of the doctrine of compulsion to hide their injustice by claiming that this injustice had been decreed by God.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
No historian tells us that the religious scholars of the time declared the killing of these Qadarites lawful, with one exception: al-Awzāʿī.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
He is said to have given Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik a legal opinion allowing him to kill Ghaylān al-Dimashqī.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
If these Qadarites had really been regarded as unbelievers or apostates from Islam, religious scholars would have permitted their killing under the rules of Islamic law.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
In fact, the attitudes of several major conservative Muslim authorities show that the Qadarites were trusted in religious matters.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Many Qadarites are known from the books of hadith as transmitters of reports from the Prophet.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The great Sunni collections, including Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, transmit hadith from a number of Qadarites just as they do from other trusted transmitters.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Even Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, founder of one of the four major Sunni schools of law, said:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“If we stopped accepting reports from the Qadarites, we would have to abandon most of the people of Basra.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This statement also tells us how widely Qadarite doctrine had spread among the educated people and intellectuals of Basra.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
From all these views about the Qadarites, we can draw one final conclusion.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
We are not claiming that Qadarite doctrine developed outside the framework of religious thought.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
What we are saying is that it made an important positive contribution to the development of opposition to Umayyad rule.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
It gave the opponents of that rule—especially the social groups suffering under Umayyad injustice—an ideology that could stand against the ideology of the Umayyad ruling class.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Its theoretical foundation was the idea that human beings possess freedom of will and are responsible for their own actions.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
That principle later became one of the foundations on which Muʿtazilite rational thought was built, as we will see in the next chapter.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
We have said that the thinkers who first developed Qadarite doctrine remained within the framework of religious thought.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
They therefore needed an Islamic religious basis for their theory of human freedom.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The Qurʾān, as the primary source of Islamic ideas, naturally became their main point of reference.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
And they did in fact find strong support in the Qurʾān for the ideas of free will and human responsibility.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Through their own interpretation of certain Qurʾānic verses, especially verses from the Meccan period, they found what they regarded as a foundation for this position.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
One account tells us about a debate between Ghaylān al-Dimashqī and the Umayyad caliph ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz over Qadarite doctrine.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
During the discussion, Ghaylān turned to the meaning of the verse:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“We have shown him the way, whether he chooses gratitude or ingratitude.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Ghaylān understood this verse to mean that God’s role is to make the path of guidance clear.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
After that, the choice belongs to the human being: either gratitude—that is, faith in this context—or unbelief.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Ghaylān therefore understood the verse as affirming that human beings have a choice in their actions and are responsible for what they choose to do.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Ghaylān, however, does not rely on Qurʾanic quotations alone. In another discussion with ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, he gives a theoretical defense of free choice based on the idea of justice. And when he applies justice to God, he treats it in a down-to-earth rather than metaphysical way, beginning with what justice means between human beings. Addressing the caliph ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Ghaylān says:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“...So consider which kind of leader you are. God does not say, ‘Come to the Fire,’ because then no one would follow Him. Those who call people to the Fire are those who call them to disobey God. Tell me, ʿUmar: have you ever known a wise man to condemn what he himself does, or to do what he condemns, or to punish people for what he has decreed, or to decree the very thing for which he punishes them? Have you ever known a merciful person to demand more of people than they are capable of, or to punish them for obeying? Have you ever known a just person to force people into injustice and wrongdoing against one another? Or a truthful person to make people lie, or make them accuse one another of lying? That should be clear enough. If someone cannot see it, that is blindness indeed.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The Qadarites also relied on many other Qurʾanic verses that seem clearly to support human freedom. For example:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“Say: The truth is from your Lord. Whoever wishes may believe, and whoever wishes may disbelieve.” — Sūrat al-Kahf, 18:29
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“There is no compulsion in religion. Right guidance has become clear from error.” — Sūrat al-Baqara, 2:256
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“Every soul is held to what it has earned.” — Sūrat al-Muddaththir, 74:38
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“Whoever follows guidance does so for his own benefit, and whoever goes astray does so to his own harm.” — Sūrat al-Isrāʾ, 17:15
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The Qadarites understood these and similar verses in a way that supported their theory of human free will, and they used them as evidence that the theory was correct.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Their reasoning was that verses of this kind contain actions, and these actions are attributed directly to human beings. In many verses, verbs such as wills, earns, follows guidance, goes astray, strives, and acts are all attributed to people themselves. The Qadarites argued that an action cannot properly be attributed to someone who had no choice in doing it. These verses must therefore point to freedom of choice.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
But the Qadarites also found other passages in the Qurʾan that seemed to point in the opposite direction. Some verses, at least on the surface, seem to support absolute predestination.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
One example appears in the discussion between ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and Ghaylān al-Dimashqī mentioned above. According to Ibn Nubāta’s account, Ghaylān quoted the verse:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“We showed him the way, whether he chooses to be grateful or ungrateful.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
ʿUmar then told him to keep reading. Ghaylān continued until he reached the words:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“This is a reminder. Whoever wishes may take a path to his Lord. But you will only if God wills.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The last part of this verse seems to deny that human beings possess a will independent of God’s will. On the surface, then, it supports absolute predestination.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Nor is it surprising that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz should accept such a view, even though he was the only Umayyad caliph commonly described as righteous or just. Good intentions alone could not naturally free him from the ideology of his family and his predecessors. That ideology was bound to shape his thinking, and perhaps his behavior as well, automatically and without any conscious intention on his part.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

The Qadarites ran into many Qurʾanic verses like the one ʿUmar quoted in his discussion with Ghaylān. These same verses were used by the supporters of predestination as evidence for their own position.

“Whomever He wishes to lead astray, He makes his chest tight and constricted.”

“God created you and what you do.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Each of these verses has its own apparent meaning.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“God is the creator of everything” would seem, by its general wording, to include human actions. A human action is itself a “thing,” so it too must have been created by God, like everything else, rather than by the human being.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“God has sealed their hearts” seems to deny freedom of the human will, because God’s will has placed its seal and its power over human hearts.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“Whomever He wishes to lead astray, He makes his chest tight and constricted” seems to say that a person goes astray because God wills it.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
And “God created you and what you do” states quite directly that God created both human beings and their actions. Everything a person does would therefore ultimately be God’s doing.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
These verses, and many others like them, clearly seem on the surface to support predestination.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
